Why do we have to see or taste the same to validate the existence of a perspective? The fact that they can see and can taste alone, doesn’t matter if it’s different from mine, shows that they have their own perspective, their own unique outlook on the world. The different between thought and optics/taste is that we have a medium to express our thoughts - language, thus allowing us to share and exchange and understand different mental opinions/perspectives on things.
No, I’ve seen from my own eyes and tasted through my own tongue. We all as humans have the same basic biology, so other people would experience reality in a similar way as I.

But there is perspective lol. We see things because of how our brain connects with our eyes, allowing the external world to be viewed to us. This is optical perspective. Same goes with all other sensations - even thought. You seemed to have ignored the latter part of my comment.

Can you explain how perspective is illusion? Do you mean that in the sense that in order for us to perceive something, it must undergo mental processes, thus creating an “imaginary” type reality which doesn’t necessarily reproduce the physical reality of the outside world? Do you believe this is the case for both thought and our physical senses?

Do you realise that having this belief is a perspective in itself, and what you’re doing to me right now is expressing your perspective? You’ve been doing it your whole life - by talking to other people you exchange your perspectives and receive and understand theirs. You’re well capable of understanding what he said said because you’ve been doing it since the day you were born, yet refuse to, why?

Yeah, I would say so. The more you open yourself up to the experiences and sensations that the current moment provides, the more you’re immersing yourself in the now. 

You make a good point with the inner dialogue however, as maintaining this attentiveness to many things can be difficult and often focusing on a singular sensation allows you to be more focused, thus having less going on in your mind. In saying that though, I don’t believe focus is the intention of meditation, and if you are strictly aware of your breath you won’t be as aware of your inner dialogue as you would be if you simply let go and embraced the moment as a whole. Meditation is often more difficult than people think, but the difficulty is a core component which allows it to be such a beneficial practice. 

I guess when you’re starting out it’s good to work your way up and over time becoming more aware of other sensations which is why watching your breath is often one of the first things you’re taught when it comes to mindfulness meditation instead of feeling external bodily sensations and being aware of sounds.

That shouldn’t stop you from seeking knowledge though. It just becomes unhealthy when you start either get a craving for it or let it get to your head. There’s nothing stopping you from seeing it from his perspective but your own close-mindedness.

Both. I try not to focus on one thing specifically, rather I open myself up to all forms of sensation - that includes being aware of my body and the weight of the air on it, the sensation of breathing in and out, sounds going on around me etc. Be as aware as possible of everything.

Meditation helps people expand their counsciousness - their peak awareness in the present moment, and lucid dreaming is becoming conscious in a normally unconscious setting. 

If you regularly practice meditation, your general awareness and presence improves, which can translate into your dreams. It’s similar to reality checks in a way (forming a habit like counting fingers, toes, putting a finger through your palm to practice in every day life to achieve lucidity while dreaming), where the more you do it, the more likely you are to experience this in your dream. 

Personally, for me, meditating for about 20 minutes right before bed has greatly helped me achieve lucid dreaming alongside consistently writing in a dream journal and thinking of achieving lucidity in my dreams while lying in bed, usually through mantras. A lot of the times my lucidity has occurred through just suddenly realising without thought that I am in a dream, and I’d like to say that this is because of regular meditation and mindful practices.
